title: Runs on every example: figures by run and model
intro: These runs follow `docs/paper_plan.md`. They were made on 2026-10-11 with three decision models: Jev, Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions. The conclusions come first. Each finding then has a page with a chart, evidence, one example and a table for the paper. The terms follow, then one table per run with the models as rows. `python scripts/report/runs_report.py paper_runs --out docs/paper_runs.html` rebuilds this document from the results folders and `scripts/definitions/paper_runs.json`. Claude Code read the figures on 2026-10-11 and wrote the conclusions and their strength. Rushab set the claim and the strength of finding 2 on 2026-10-11. Rushab has not reviewed the others.
conclusions: The claim. A decision model gives each option in a list a probability. That probability does not reliably say whether the option is correct. It is close to the accuracy when exactly one option in the list is correct. It is not close in the three other cases.

Several correct options (finding 2, the main finding). When 2 to 4 options in a list are correct, one of them has a mean probability of 0.66 to 0.85. The correct option with the lowest probability has 0.11 to 0.19. This happens on three datasets and three models. TypeSafe's example code notifies a second team when its probability is above 0.25. Every correct option is above 0.25 in 15% to 35% of the answers. Strong.

TypeSafe's example (finding 6). TypeSafe's example ticket has two issues. Jev gives their two teams 0.65 and 0.31. The documentation shows 0.61 and 0.35. On 24 tickets written the same way, both teams are above 0.25 in 11 tickets on Jev, 12 on Liquid d1 and 3 on GPT-6 Luna Decisions. When an issue is sent alone, the models give its team 0.99 to 1.00. Moderate: 24 tickets.

Why the second correct option is low (finding 5). Remove the correct option with the highest probability from the list. The second correct option then rises from between 0.11 and 0.19 to between 0.53 and 0.71. Sharing out the removed probability in proportion predicts this rise. Liquid d1 returns full-precision probabilities: the prediction is 0.64, 0.80 and 0.70 on the three datasets, and the model gives 0.61, 0.70 and 0.67. Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions return 2 decimals, and their values agree within 0.13 on the examples where 0.10 or more is left. This supports finding 2. It is not a finding of its own.

Identical options (finding 1). In a list of 5 copies of one correct option, every copy is equally correct, and equal probabilities are 0.20. Jev gives its highest copy 0.29 to 0.34 and its lowest copy 0.10 to 0.12. Liquid d1 gives them 0.50 to 0.81 and 0.03 to 0.08. GPT-6 Luna Decisions gives them 0.67 to 0.79 and 0.01 to 0.02. Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions pick the first copy in 86% to 100% of their answers. Strong.

No correct option (finding 3). When no option in a list is correct, Jev and Liquid d1 answer every list. Their mean confidence is 0.49 to 0.87. GPT-6 Luna Decisions refuses 58% to 98% of the lists with random options. It refuses 1% to 27% of the lists with the example's distractors. Strong for random options.

One correct option (finding 4). The mean confidence is within 0.14 of the accuracy. The probability works in this case. When several options are correct, the mean confidence is 0.08 to 0.23 below the accuracy.

For the paper. Finding 2 carries the paper. Finding 6 tests it on TypeSafe's own example. Findings 1 and 3 show two more cases where the probability does not say whether an option is correct. Each request was sent once. No figure has a margin of error yet.

findings.title: 1. Identical options: the copies do not get equal probabilities, and the position decides which copy gets the most
findings.conclusion: A list of 5 copies of one correct option has no better option, and equal probabilities are 0.20 each. No model gives equal probabilities. Jev gives its highest copy 0.29 to 0.34 and its lowest copy 0.10 to 0.12. Liquid d1 gives them 0.50 to 0.81 and 0.03 to 0.08, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions 0.67 to 0.79 and 0.01 to 0.02. The position decides which copy is highest.
findings.strength: strong for the three models. Identical options get different probabilities: the highest copy is ahead of the lowest copy by 0.17 to 0.23 on Jev, 0.42 to 0.78 on Liquid d1 and 0.65 to 0.78 on GPT-6 Luna Decisions. Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions put the highest copy first. Jev's preferred position changes with the dataset.
evidence: Jev gives the highest copy a mean of 0.32, 0.33, 0.34 and 0.29 on MetaTool, MMLU, HotpotQA and ECtHR, and the lowest copy 0.11, 0.10, 0.11 and 0.12. The highest copy gets 2.4 to 3.3 times the probability of the lowest copy.

Liquid d1 gives the highest copy 0.81, 0.50, 0.73 and 0.55, and the lowest copy 0.03, 0.08, 0.04 and 0.07. GPT-6 Luna Decisions gives the highest copy 0.78, 0.74, 0.79 and 0.67, and the lowest copy 0.02, 0.01, 0.01 and 0.02.
The highest copy is ahead of the second-highest copy by 0.06 to 0.11 on Jev, 0.31 to 0.73 on Liquid d1 and 0.45 to 0.68 on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
The mean entropy is 1.03 to 1.85 bits on Liquid d1, 1.00 to 1.35 bits on GPT-6 Luna Decisions and 2.18 to 2.24 bits on Jev. Equal probabilities give 2.32 bits.

Liquid d1 picks position 1 in 99.9%, 85.7%, 99.5% and 99.6% of answers on MetaTool, MMLU, HotpotQA and ECtHR, respectively. GPT-6 Luna Decisions picks it in 98.6%, 87.8%, 99.4% and 98.9% of answers, respectively. An equal share is 20%.
Jev picks the last position in 73.9% of answers on MMLU, 59.3% on ECtHR, 35.5% on MetaTool and 29.5% on HotpotQA.
With 5 paraphrases of one MetaTool tool, Liquid d1 picks position 1 in 74% of answers. GPT-6 Luna Decisions picks it in 87% of answers, and Jev in 26%.

With one correct tool among distractors, GPT-6 Luna Decisions has an accuracy of 0.80 when the tool is first and 0.67 when it is last. Jev's accuracy goes from 0.78 to 0.80, and Liquid d1's from 0.69 to 0.74.
Each model received 30,695 lists across four datasets. Each list appeared in its 5 cyclic permutations.
limits: The copies' names differ by extra spaces. The API needs those spaces to tell them apart.

A user does not send a list of identical options. The run with one correct tool among distractors connects this test to real lists. There, the effect is 0.13 for one model and 0.05 or less for the two others.
Each request was sent once. Jev does not always give the same answer to the same request.

findings.title: 2. Allocation: the model gives most of the probability to one of several correct options
findings.conclusion: When a list has 2 to 4 correct options, the models give most of the probability to one of them: a mean of 0.66 to 0.85. The lowest correct option gets 0.11 to 0.19. The highest distractor gets 0.04 to 0.17, and the two ranges overlap. Asking for both options does not change this. On Jev, "Choose both." gives the lowest correct MetaTool tool 0.15, and "Choose one of them." gives it 0.14.
findings.strength: strong, and the paper's main finding. TypeSafe's documentation reads 0.61 and 0.35 as a ticket for two teams. Its example code notifies a second team above 0.25. Across three datasets and three models, every correct option is above 0.25 in 15% to 35% of answers. Someone who follows that rule misses a correct option in 65% to 85% of these lists.
evidence: On MetaTool, the mean probabilities for the highest and lowest correct options are 0.85 and 0.11 for Jev, 0.71 and 0.16 for Liquid d1, and 0.66 and 0.11 for GPT-6 Luna Decisions. On HotpotQA, the same models give 0.77 and 0.17, 0.74 and 0.19, and 0.72 and 0.15. On ECtHR, they give 0.72 and 0.15, 0.72 and 0.16, and 0.73 and 0.13.

On MetaTool, every correct option is above 0.25 in 15% of Jev's answers, 27% of Liquid d1's answers, and 16% of GPT-6 Luna Decisions' answers. In the same model order, this happens in 30%, 35% and 26% of HotpotQA answers, and in 23%, 25% and 17% of ECtHR answers.

TypeSafe's primer says outcomes with a probability of `0.2` should happen about 20% of the time. The models give the lowest correct option a mean probability of 0.11 to 0.19. The dataset labels it correct in every one of these lists.

On average, the lowest correct option is 0.05 to 0.14 above the highest distractor. For GPT-6 Luna Decisions on MetaTool, it is 0.06 below. A probability threshold does not separate the second correct option from the distractors.
The models usually rank the options correctly. The prediction is a correct option in 0.82 to 0.98 of answers. The 2 highest options are the 2 correct ones in 0.52 to 0.85 of answers.

With Jev on MetaTool, "Choose one of them." gives the lowest correct tool 0.14, and "Choose both." gives it 0.15. On HotpotQA, "may support", "supports" and "definitely supports" give the lowest supporting passage 0.18, 0.17 and 0.17.

Finding 5 explains the cause. Finding 6 tests TypeSafe's example. When an issue is sent alone, the model gives its team 0.99 to 1.00. When the ticket has a second issue, the team with the lower probability gets 0.12 to 0.28 on average.
The results cover 7,405 HotpotQA questions, 497 MetaTool queries and 192 ECtHR cases.
limits: TypeSafe's documentation gives the 0.25 threshold. It does not say what probabilities two correct options should get. The finding is that this threshold misses correct options. It does not say that 0.50 each is the right answer.
HotpotQA labels a passage when it has a supporting sentence. The passage may be needed to answer the question even if it does not support the answer on its own, as finding 5's yes/no questions show.
The ECtHR labels show the Court's findings. They do not cover every article related to the case facts.

findings.title: 3. Abstention: confident answers to lists with no correct option
findings.conclusion: Jev and Liquid d1 answer every list with no correct option. Their confidence is close to their confidence on lists with one correct option. GPT-6 Luna Decisions returns an answer of type `refusal` for many lists with no correct option. On the lists it answers, its confidence is as high as Jev's and Liquid d1's. When NOTA is offered, the three models pick it for random options. They pick it less often for the example's distractors.
findings.strength: strong for lists of random options, where no option can be correct. Moderate for the example's distractors, where the label says no option is correct. The vendor does not document GPT-6 Luna Decisions' refusals.
evidence: On lists of 5 random options, Jev's mean confidence is 0.78, 0.55 and 0.58 on MetaTool, MMLU and HotpotQA. Liquid d1's is 0.74, 0.60 and 0.49 in the same order.

On four datasets, Jev's mean confidence is 0.61 to 0.83 on lists of the example's distractors. Liquid d1's is 0.67 to 0.87. On lists with one correct option, Jev's is 0.86 to 0.94 and Liquid d1's is 0.81 to 0.89.

GPT-6 Luna Decisions refuses 58%, 85% and 98% of lists with random options. It refuses 23%, 6%, 27% and 1% of lists with the example's distractors. Jev and Liquid d1 refuse none of 202,088 questions each.

When lists have NOTA and random options, the models predict NOTA in 0.93 to 1.00 of their answers. With NOTA and the example's distractors, they predict it in 0.54 to 0.72 of answers on MMLU and 0.79 to 0.88 on HotpotQA. For ECtHR cases with no violated article, they predict NOTA in 0.37, 0.07 and 0.17 of answers.

One request with a refused list was sent again 7 times, with one change each time. The model answered the same passages when the query was changed to one that a passage fits. It answered the same query when NOTA or a fitting passage was added to the list.
limits: A MetaTool example's distractors can include a tool that fits the query. The run's label was read for only 50 queries.
In an ECtHR case with no label, the Court found no violation. The case's facts can still point to an article.
GPT-6 Luna Decisions answers 2% to 99% of the lists. Its figures cover only the lists it answers.
No source says why the model refuses. The API gives no reason.

findings.title: 4. Calibration: confidence is close to accuracy with one correct option, but the result does not carry over
findings.conclusion: On lists with one correct option, the three models' confidence is close to their accuracy. With several correct options, their confidence is 0.08 to 0.23 below their accuracy. With none, their confidence is 0.49 to 0.87. A confidence threshold set on one kind of list does not hold on another. With several correct options, a yes/no question per option gives each option a probability. On MetaTool, the tools given more than 0.70 for yes are correct in 76% to 77% of the answers, at mean probabilities of yes of 0.83 to 0.96.
findings.strength: the case in which the probability works, not a finding on its own. The figures are sound. The gaps on the other lists follow from findings 2 and 3. A shared probability lowers confidence, and a list with no correct option has accuracy 0.
evidence: With one correct option, mean confidence minus accuracy is +0.08, +0.09 and +0.14 on MetaTool for Jev, Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions. It is +0.02, +0.05 and +0.04 on MMLU, and -0.03, -0.01 and 0.00 on ECtHR.
With several correct options, mean confidence minus accuracy is -0.12, -0.16 and -0.08 on MetaTool. It is -0.19, -0.21 and -0.20 on HotpotQA, and -0.21, -0.23 and -0.21 on ECtHR.
With one correct option, ECE with 10 bins ranges from 0.01 to 0.15.

With a yes/no question per option, the answers above 0.70 for yes are about a correct option in 76% to 94% of the cases, at mean probabilities of yes of 0.78 to 0.96. The answers from 0.20 to 0.40 are about a correct option in 13% to 54% of the cases, at mean probabilities of 0.28 to 0.33.

On the 401 HotpotQA bridge questions, passages given a mean probability of yes of 0.28 to 0.29 are supporting passages in 48% to 52% of the answers, and passages given 0.87 to 0.93 in 77% to 82%. The share of supporting passages rises from bin to bin for every model.
The analysis includes 16,770 MetaTool lists, 4,000 MMLU lists and 6,550 ECtHR lists with one correct option.
limits: Rushab, 2026-10-14: calibration of a list's probabilities is not defined when several options are correct, since the probabilities of a list sum to 1. With several correct options, only the yes/no questions are used.
The 5 bins of the yes/no answers have edges 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7 and 1.0, so that each bin holds 50 or more answers. They hold 51 to 3,895.
Accuracy counts a prediction as correct when it is one of the correct options. With several correct options, a different definition gives a different gap.
MetaTool labels one tool per query. On some queries, the three models agree on a different answer, as in the example.
No interval has been computed yet.

findings.title: 5. Removal: the second correct option has a low probability because the first has most of it
findings.conclusion: An option's probability is its share of the list. It does not judge that option alone. When the correct option with the highest probability is removed, the second correct option gets most of that option's probability. Dividing the removed probability among the remaining options in proportion gives nearly the same value.
findings.strength: supports finding 2. It is not a separate finding. Probabilities in a list sum to 1, so the remaining options' probabilities rise when one is removed. Liquid d1 returns probabilities with full precision. Dividing its second correct option's probability in the full list by the probability of the remaining options gives 0.64, 0.80 and 0.70 on MetaTool, HotpotQA and ECtHR. After the removal, Liquid d1 gives 0.61, 0.70 and 0.67. Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions return 2 decimals, so their division is less exact. Across the three models, the two values are within 0.13 of each other in each of the nine cells.
evidence: On MetaTool, Jev's probability for the second correct option goes from 0.11 to 0.71, Liquid d1's from 0.16 to 0.62, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions' from 0.11 to 0.53 after removal. On HotpotQA, their probabilities go from 0.17 to 0.66, 0.19 to 0.68 and 0.16 to 0.60. On ECtHR, they go from 0.19 to 0.71, 0.16 to 0.68 and 0.15 to 0.68.

On the examples where the options other than the removed one hold 0.10 or more, the second correct option's renormalised probability is 0.77, 0.64 and 0.40 on MetaTool for Jev, Liquid d1 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions. It is 0.80, 0.80 and 0.61 on HotpotQA, and 0.72, 0.70 and 0.59 on ECtHR. After the removal, the same examples give 0.72, 0.61 and 0.49 on MetaTool, 0.67, 0.70 and 0.60 on HotpotQA, and 0.71, 0.67 and 0.68 on ECtHR.
When one correct option is removed, the models predict the remaining correct option in 0.86, 0.78 and 0.67 of the MetaTool answers and in 0.84, 0.84 and 0.80 of the HotpotQA answers.
In a yes/no question about a correct MetaTool tool alone, the models give yes a mean probability of 0.64, 0.79 and 0.65. They give 66% to 85% of those tools 0.50 or more for yes.
In a yes/no question about a violated ECtHR article alone, the models give yes a mean probability of 0.67, 0.89 and 0.74. They give 80% to 96% of those articles 0.50 or more for yes.
When asked about a supporting HotpotQA passage alone, the models give it 0.45, 0.40 and 0.52. They give 38% to 51% of those passages 0.50 or more.
limits: Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions return probabilities with 2 decimals. Dividing by a remainder near 0.01 means little at 2 decimals. The renormalised value therefore uses only the examples where the remaining options hold 0.10 or more. On Jev these are 227 of 497 MetaTool queries, 4,866 of 7,384 HotpotQA questions and 150 of 192 ECtHR cases.
The HotpotQA yes/no figures show that about half of the supporting passages are not judged to support the answer alone. This weakens the view that both passages are correct options.
HotpotQA's yes/no questions cover 500 questions.

findings.title: 6. The documented example: a ticket for two teams
findings.conclusion: TypeSafe's Choice documentation shows a ticket about a wrong size and a double charge. It gives returns 0.61 and billing 0.35, and says the ticket belongs to two teams. Its example code notifies a second team when its probability is above 0.25. Jev gives that answer again. Across 24 similar tickets, the rule finds the second team in about half of the tickets on Jev and Liquid d1, and in 3 tickets on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
findings.strength: moderate: 24 tickets. It is the direct test of finding 2 on TypeSafe's documented example. The documented answer holds, so the paper cannot say the example is wrong. The rule in the example code is not reliable. On Jev, a team gets 1.00 when its issue is sent alone, and below 0.25 in 13 of 24 tickets with a second issue.
evidence: TypeSafe's example request was sent once on 2026-10-11. Jev gives returns 0.65, billing 0.31 and shipping 0.04. The documentation shows returns 0.61, billing 0.35 and shipping 0.04. Liquid d1 gives returns 0.20, billing 0.75 and shipping 0.05. GPT-6 Luna Decisions gives returns 0.49, billing 0.50 and shipping 0.01.

For 24 tickets with two issues, Jev gives the higher of the two teams a mean probability of 0.76 and the lower one 0.24. Liquid d1 gives them 0.71 and 0.28. GPT-6 Luna Decisions gives them 0.87 and 0.12.
The second team is above 0.25 in 11 of 24 tickets on Jev, 12 tickets on Liquid d1 and 3 tickets on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
The same 24 issues were sent one per ticket. Each issue's team gets a mean probability of 1.00 on Jev, 0.99 on Liquid d1 and 1.00 on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
The team neither issue concerns gets 0.00 to 0.01. The models separate it from the two teams that apply, but give those two teams different probabilities.
Changing the order of the two issues changes the prediction in 1 of 12 pairs on Jev, 4 pairs on Liquid d1 and 3 pairs on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
TypeSafe's ticket also mentions a late delivery. Shipping gets 0.04 on Jev, 0.05 on Liquid d1 and 0.01 on GPT-6 Luna Decisions.
limits: Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the 24 issues on 2026-10-11. No second reader checked that each issue concerns only one team.
The two issues in a ticket may not matter equally. No reference gives the right split.
Each request was sent once. When the team question from TypeSafe's ticket was sent again during the ticket run, Jev gave 0.58 and 0.37.
This test uses one vendor's example and three teams. The four datasets in findings 1 to 5 support the general claim.

terms: an entry in the list sent with a query. It is a tool on MetaTool, a choice on MMLU, a passage on HotpotQA, or an article on ECtHR.
an option the dataset labels as correct for the query.
an option that is not a correct option.

an option that says no other option is correct. It is "None" on MetaTool, "None of the above" on MMLU, "None of the passages" on HotpotQA, and "None of these articles" on ECtHR. NOTA is the correct option when the list has no other correct option.
the option the model picks in the `choice` field of its answer.
the highest probability in an answer. It is not the `confidence` field of the model's answer.
a list for which the model returns an answer of type `refusal` and no probabilities.
the share of answers whose prediction is a correct option.
for a list with k correct options, where k is 2 or more, the share of answers whose k options with the highest probabilities are the k correct options. A tie for place k does not count as a match.

the answers go into 10 bins by confidence, from 0 to 0.1 through 0.9 to 1.0. Each bin has a distance between its mean confidence and its accuracy. ECE averages the 10 distances, weighted by the number of answers in each bin.
the highest probability in an answer minus the second-highest probability.
the highest probability of a correct option minus the lowest probability of a correct option.
the highest probability of a correct option minus the highest probability of a distractor.
the lowest probability of a correct option minus the highest probability of a distractor. It is negative when a distractor has a higher probability than a correct option.

the sum of -p log2(p) for every probability p in an answer, in bits. It is 0 when one option has 1.00. Its maximum is log2 of the number of options. The maximum occurs when every option has the same probability, and the column header shows it.
an option's place in the list sent to the model, counting from the first.
notes: Jev is `jev-1.13.0` and uses TypeSafe's API. Liquid d1 (`liquid/d1`) and GPT-6 Luna Decisions (`openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions`) use Vercel AI Gateway, which does not take a model version. All three models get the same requests.
Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions return each probability with 2 decimals. Liquid d1 returns full floating-point values.
Every figure in a row uses the lists that the model answered. A refused list has no answer. Jev and Liquid d1 refused no lists.
A table leaves out a column when no model has that figure. A list with no correct option has no accuracy. A list with only correct options has no distractor.

The three differences and the probabilities are calculated for each answer, then averaged across answers. Differences involving a distractor use answers to lists with a correct option and a distractor. When a run also has lists with only correct options, the column "Lists with a correct option and a distractor" shows how many lists have both.

The MMLU runs use a seeded sample of 1,000 of the 13,096 questions whose choices can be moved. The HotpotQA runs with 5 cyclic permutations and the HotpotQA run with 4 distractors and NOTA use a seeded sample of 1,000 of the 7,345 questions with 10 passages. The other runs use every example.

MetaTool repeats queries across its test files. The run with paraphrases has 1,767 examples and 1,047 different requests. The run with duplicates has 3,292 examples and 3,275 different requests. An answer to a repeated request counts once per example.
ECtHR labels name the articles that the Court found violated in a case. A case with no label means the Court found no violation of the 10 articles.

The test sends a yes/no question about each tool of the 497 MetaTool multi-tool queries, run on 2026-10-14. It sends a yes/no question about each HotpotQA passage for 500 questions, and about each ECtHR article for the 1,000 test cases.
The file `src/grjev/stimuli/tickets.json` has the tickets, TypeSafe's example request, and its documented answer. `python scripts/run/typesafe_example.py` sends that request.
